 Mahanadi IPO: Coal India's best mine, priced for no growth
 Coal India's most profitable subsidiary lists at 8.4 times earnings. That looks cheap, but its profits have shrunk for two years and the price reflects it.
 Lakshya Naredi • November 17, 2026 
 --> 
 SHARE
 AI-generated image 
 हिंदी में भी पढ़ें 
 Summary: It is the biggest producer in the Coal India family and keeps more of every rupee than its parent does. Yet the market is being asked to price it as though its best days are already behind it. Whether that is a bargain or a fair warning depends on how you plan to own it.
 Mahanadi Coalfields is arguably the best business within Coal India . In FY26, it produced 218 million tonnes of coal, more than any other company in India, and earned a net profit of Rs 10,698 crore. That is nearly 35 per cent of Coal India's consolidated profit, despite contributing less than a fifth of its revenue.
 Now, Coal India is selling 10 per cent of the subsidiary to public investors. At the upper price band of Rs 136, Mahanadi is valued at around Rs 90,010 crore, or 8.4 times its FY26 earnings.
 That looks cheap for a company with a 35 per cent net profit margin and a 53.9 per cent return on net worth. But there is a catch. Revenue and profit have both declined for two consecutive years, and coal prices are largely controlled by its parent. The IPO raises a simple question: how much should investors pay for a cash-generating business that has stopped growing?
 The issue is entirely an offer for sale, so Mahanadi will not receive any of the IPO proceeds.
 How Mahanadi makes money 
 Mahanadi's business is simple: it mines non-coking coal in Odisha and sells most of it to power plants.
 It operates 17 mines across the Talcher and Ib Valley coalfields, of which 14 are open-cast mines. These mines are generally cheaper to operate than underground mines because machines remove the soil and rock above the coal before extracting it.
 Mahanadi also outsources much of its mining activity. Contractors produced 157 million tonnes of its coal in FY26 and removed 88 per cent of its overburden. This keeps its permanent workforce relatively lean and makes a larger portion of its costs flexible.
 Thermal power plants accounted for 68.6 per cent of coal sales in FY26. Around 82 per cent of sales came through long-term fuel supply agreements, with prices largely determined by Coal India's notified rates. This provides demand visibility but limits Mahanadi's pricing independence.
 Mahanadi's efficiency becomes clearer when compared with South Eastern Coalfields (SECL), another large Coal India subsidiary, and Coal India itself.
 SECL produced 176.3 million tonnes of coal in FY26 and generated higher revenue than Mahanadi. Yet its net profit was less than half.

 The striking observation is that Mahanadi earns the least revenue per tonne but retains the most profit. The difference comes largely from its cost structure.
 A leaner workforce. Mahanadi produces 10,636 tonnes of coal per permanent employee, against 4,958 tonnes at SECL and 3,622 tonnes for Coal India. Employee expenses account for just 15.5 per cent of Mahanadi's revenue, compared with 27.6 per cent for Coal India. Its greater reliance on contractors also makes costs more flexible when mining activity slows.
 Favourable geology. Mahanadi removes just 1.5 cubic metres of overburden (the soil and rock removed to reach the coal) for every tonne of coal extracted. SECL removes 2.06 cubic metres and Coal India 2.58. Less excavation means lower mining costs. SECL also operates 34 underground mines, compared with just three at Mahanadi.
 Strengths and risks 
 Mahanadi's biggest strength is its low-cost operating structure. Its mining conditions, open-cast operations and lean workforce make it better placed than many peers to withstand pressure on coal prices.
 It also has virtually no debt, with borrowings of just Rs 3 crore as of March 2026. Its 53.9 per cent return on net worth reflects its ability to generate substantial profits without much additional capital.
 However, there are risks.
 Parent dependence. Coal India owns 90 per cent of Mahanadi and controls the pricing framework for most of its coal. The parent also has considerable influence over dividend decisions. Minority shareholders will have a direct stake in the subsidiary but little control over its capital allocation.
 Potential mineral levy exposure. Coal India's legal team estimates Mahanadi's possible exposure to state mineral levies at Rs 31,228 crore, nearly three times its FY26 profit. This is not a confirmed demand or a recognised balance-sheet liability, but the CAG has questioned its disclosure. Any substantial eventual payment could affect the company's financial position.
 Rising coal inventory. Unsold coal at Mahanadi's mines increased from 36.8 million tonnes to 43.8 million tonnes in FY26, accounting for nearly a third of Coal India's total unsold inventory. High stocks at power plants can weaken fresh demand and e-auction premiums.
 Limited growth prospects. Renewable energy poses a longer-term challenge to coal demand. Moreover, Mahanadi's top 10 customers accounted for 55.9 per cent of revenue, making it dependent on a relatively concentrated customer base.
 Our verdict: treat it like a bond 
 Mahanadi makes the most sense if you see it as a bond that pays you every year, not a stock that should grow. At the top of the band, each Rs 100 invested is backed by about Rs 12 of yearly profit, and Mahanadi paid out 72 per cent of its FY26 profit as dividends. If profit merely holds steady, that is about Rs 8.50 a year in cash on every Rs 100.
 But this bond has no fixed payment and no promise to return your money. The payment depends on prices set by the parent and on power plants already full of coal.
 So the question is not whether Mahanadi is a good business. It is. The question is whether 8 to 9 per cent a year in cash pays you enough for those risks.
